screens.title: Running on Fumes
screens.sub: Meet your nervous system, and learn two breaths to carry with you

screens.title: Before we begin

blocks.p: About 15 minutes: two short videos, two practices, and a couple of places to write. Writing is always optional.
Some of this is quiet, and quiet can stir things up. Stop whenever you like. The Pause button is always there.

blocks.h: Start only if you are steady today
blocks.p: If today is rough, come back tomorrow. That is the whole skill.
It is not therapy, and the AI reflections are not me. If you are in crisis, call or text 988, or call 911.

screens.lead: I send this when I think it will help, usually a couple of weeks into our work. Not everyone gets every course, and that is on purpose.
screens.note: Your notes stay on your device. Next, you choose whether I ever see them.

screens.title: Your body's gas and brake
frames: Your nervous system has a gas pedal and a brake.
The gas revs you up to meet something. The brake slows you down so you can rest and recover.
Regulation is using both smoothly, so your energy matches the moment. That middle zone is your window of tolerance, a phrase from Dr. Dan Siegel.
After months of stress, the gas can stick. Racing, wired, on edge.
Or the brake can slam on. Flat, foggy, heavy. Burnout often swings between the two.
Regulation also includes the way back: easing off one pedal, a little at a time.
screens.note: Nothing here is about being calm all the time. It is about having both pedals work, and finding your way back to the middle.

screens.title: Where is your body right now?
screens.prompt: No right answer. Pick the closest one. This is a ten-second check you can do any time.

revved.text: Thank you for telling the truth about it. Revved up wants to come down a notch before it can think. The cooling breath later in this course is made for this.
revved.label: Skip ahead to the cooling breath

window.text: Good. This is a fine moment to learn something new, so keep going.

low.text: Okay. Powered down needs a different kind of help. Slow and gentle. You can skip the cooling breath, and the last screen has a guided half-minute that suits this.
low.label: Skip ahead to coming back to now

unsure.text: That counts. "I can't tell" is an honest state, and often it means a bit of both.

screens.title: Welcome: why regulation comes first
screens.summary: Why I start with the body, what flooding looks like in burnout, and how to use this course alongside our sessions.
bullets: Why the nervous system, and not just "rest more"
What regulation means, in plain words
How this fits with our sessions

screens.title: What happens in your body when the alarm goes off
frames: Your brain has a smoke alarm. Its job is to notice danger fast, before you have time to think.
When it goes off, your body gets ready. Heart speeds up, muscles brace, breath goes shallow. That is the gas pedal.
When the alarm is very loud, the thinking part of your brain works less well. Words get hard, memory gets patchy, and everything feels urgent. This is flooding.
Flooding can also be quiet. The brake slams on and things go numb, foggy, or far away. Same cause, different direction.
The alarm can be told it is safe. A long exhale, your feet on the floor, and looking around the room all send that message. The thinking brain comes back.

screens.title: Flooding

cards.p: Racing and wired, or blank and far away. Both are the alarm system pushed past your window.
While you are flooded, calming the body works better than talking it through. That is why this course starts with regulation and goes in small doses.

cards.h: A note about the AI helper
cards.p: If you write something big here, the helper will gently point you to a real person. That is not rejection of you or your story. When someone is flooded, a calmer body and a human come first.

screens.intro: Flooding is what you just saw: feelings, or shutdown, arriving faster than your thinking can keep up. It is not a flaw. It is a nervous system doing its job.

screens.title: The parts that got you here

cards.p: Keeps you moving. "Just one more thing." It is afraid of what happens if you stop.
Says yes before you have checked. It keeps everyone okay, because that once helped you stay safe.
Says no by shutting everything down. It looks like laziness. It is an emergency brake.

screens.intro: Parts language is just a way of describing the different reactions we all have. You do not have to take it literally.
screens.eyebrow: A kinder way to talk about it
screens.note: None of them is the enemy. They are working double shifts.

screens.title: Who has been running the show?
screens.prompt: Which of those sounds most familiar, or what would you call yours? What does it say on a hard day?
screens.helper: No need to explain where it came from. Just notice what it does.
screens.placeholder: For example: my Driver says that if I stop, everything falls apart...

screens.title: Two breaths: a practice and a tool
screens.summary: How I think about practice versus tools, why small doses beat big efforts, and a quick tour of the toning breath and the cooling breath.
bullets: Practice when you are steady, tool when you are not
When the cooling breath helps, and when to skip it

screens.title: The three-part toning breath
steps: Sit or stand with your feet on the floor. Eyes open or softly closed, whichever feels better.
Breathe in through your nose in three small sips. First low in the belly, then the ribs, then the top of your chest.
Breathe out slowly with a soft hum, an "mmm" or a "voo". Let the sound fade to the very end of the breath. Keep your jaw loose, like a purr.
Repeat for five rounds. Then rest and breathe normally for a moment.
screens.lead: This is for when you are steady enough, as a regular habit. Think of it as brushing your teeth, for your nervous system.
cautions: Never strain. The breath and the hum both stay easy.
No breath holds in this one.
If you feel dizzy, tingly, or uneasy, stop and breathe normally. Look around the room. That is useful information, not a failure.
If breathing exercises are hard for you, skip this and tell me. There are other ways in.
screens.note: Many people find a long, humming out-breath settles them. It does not work the same for everyone, and it is not magic. We are running an experiment on you, with you.

screens.title: What did you notice?
screens.prompt: Anything shift, even a little? A sensation, a thought, a softening. Or nothing at all, which counts too.
screens.placeholder: For example: my jaw let go a little on the third hum...

screens.title: The cooling breath
steps: Curl your tongue into a tube and sip air through it, like a straw. If you cannot curl your tongue, purse your lips as if sipping through a straw. Feel the cool air.
Close your mouth and breathe out slowly through your nose, longer than the sip in.
Do six rounds. Then breathe normally and notice. Cooler? Steadier? The same? All of that is fine.
screens.lead: For when you are hot, wired, snappy, or spinning. Think of it as a small fan for your nervous system.
screens.eyebrow: A tool for when you are revved up
cautions: Skip it if cool air bothers your chest, or if you are sick or having an asthma flare. A slow breath out is plenty.
Skip it if you are powered down, flat, or sleepy. It can push you lower. Use feet, seat, room instead.
If it makes you more anxious, stop. Tell me about it in session.

screens.title: If you notice flooding
steps: Stop what you are doing. Noticing is the skill, and you just did it.
Feel your feet. Look around slowly. Say today's date.
Breathe normally. If it feels okay, let the out-breath run a little longer.
Come back to the course later, or tell me.
screens.lead: Flooding can be loud or quiet. Either way, the first move is the same: slow down and come back to now.

guide.text: Let your eyes move slowly around the room.
Find something you like the look of. Rest your eyes on it.
Feel your feet. Press them down a little.
Say, out loud or in your head: "It is today. I am here."

screens.guideEnd: Good. Notice if anything is even a little different.
screens.note: If you write something big in this course, the AI helper will point you to a real person. That is not a rejection. When you are flooded, a calmer body and a human come first. If you ever feel unsafe, call or text 988, or call 911.
